title: Parents once mailed their kid with 53 cents in stamps
hook: In 1914, a five-year-old was sent by parcel post

open.title: Why the US Post Office accepted a five-year-old as a parcel
open.line: February 1914: an Idaho post office took in a five-year-old package.

summary: When US parcel post began in 1913, no rule banned mailing people. In 1914, five-year-old May was mailed to her grandparents with 53 cents in stamps on her sleeve.

text: On February 19, 1914, five-year-old May was mailed as a parcel.
The 53 cents in stamps went on her sleeve.
From Grangeville, Idaho, to her grandparents in Lewiston.
She weighed 48.5 pounds. The parcel limit was 50.
US parcel post started on January 1, 1913.
No rule anywhere said you couldn't mail a person.
May rode in the mail car of the train,
with a railway post office clerk beside her.
Actually, May wasn't even the first.
Weeks after parcel post opened, a baby in Ohio got mailed.
The baby weighed 10 and three quarter pounds.
His parents paid 15 cents in stamps and insured him for 50 dollars.
After May, the Postmaster General told post offices nationwide: no humans in the mail.
The next year, six-year-old Edna was mailed by train from Florida to Virginia.

sources: National Postal Museum: The Oddest Parcels
National Postal Museum: 250 Years of Stamps and Stories, 1910s
